questions.question: What are type annotations in Python, and how do you use the basic ones?
questions.title: Basic Type Annotations in Python
questions.direct_answer: Type annotations describe the type a variable, parameter, or return value is expected to have. Python records these hints but does not enforce them by default at runtime; editors and static checkers such as mypy use them to find mismatches before execution.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the variable, parameter, and return syntax and understand the boundary between a type hint and a runtime check.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming that writing an annotation makes Python reject a wrong value while the program is running.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect the syntax to static analysis and state the Python 3.9 and 3.10 boundaries for modern collection and union syntax.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Write a variable hint as `name: str = "Ada"`.
Write parameter hints after `:` and a return hint after `->`.
Python stores annotations but does not check argument or assignment types by default.
Use an editor or a static checker such as mypy to turn the hints into useful feedback.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Type annotations are labels that describe what type of value a name is expected to hold. A variable can be written as `age: int = 24`, while `def greet(name: str) -> str` describes both the parameter and the result.

They do not turn Python into a statically executed language. Python normally records the annotations and continues to use dynamic runtime types, so passing an `int` to a parameter marked `str` is not automatically rejected at the call boundary.

A static checker such as mypy reads those labels without running the program. For example, it can flag `greet(42)` because the call disagrees with the declared contract, and an IDE can use the same information for completion and safe refactoring.

I annotate public functions, data models, and values whose type is not obvious. I usually let a checker infer simple locals such as `total = 0`, because repeating `total: int = 0` adds little information.

For current Python, collection hints use forms such as `list[str]` from Python 3.9 and unions can use `str | None` from Python 3.10. Older supported versions may require `typing.List` or `typing.Optional`.

sections.title: The contract exists beside the runtime value
sections.content:
Python still decides an object's actual type from the object created at runtime. An annotation adds a second layer: a declared contract that tools can compare with the values flowing through the program. The contract is useful before execution, but it does not replace tests, input validation, or error handling.

Function annotations are available through `__annotations__`; tools that need resolved hints can use `typing.get_type_hints()`. This runtime visibility lets frameworks use annotations for features such as dependency injection or validation, but that behaviour comes from the framework—not from ordinary Python assignment or function calls.

Use `-> None` for a function that finishes without returning a useful value. It tells a checker that callers must not treat its result as data. An unannotated value is not necessarily unknown: a checker can infer many simple types from assignments, so the best annotations clarify boundaries rather than label every line.

sections.title: Who reads a type annotation?
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  S[Python source with annotations] --> P[Python runtime]
  S --> T[Static checker or IDE]
  P --> V[Creates and uses real objects]
  T --> C[Compares expected and inferred types]
  C --> W[Reports a warning before execution]
  V -. no automatic boundary check .-> W
```

sections.title: Annotate a value and a complete function
sections.content:
```python
name: str = "Ada"
visits: int = 3
active: bool = True

def build_label(name: str, visits: int) -> str:
    return f"{name} ({visits})"

label: str = build_label(name, visits)
print(label)
print(build_label.__annotations__)
```

This runs normally and prints the label plus the stored annotation dictionary. A checker can also verify that every call and return agrees with the declared types.

questions.question: Where do type annotations add the most value, and when is type inference enough?
questions.title: Choosing Useful Python Type Annotations
questions.direct_answer: Annotations add the most value at module boundaries, public functions, data models, and places where a value's shape is not obvious. Inference is usually enough for simple local expressions when the assigned value already makes the type clear.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can use annotations deliberately instead of treating maximum annotation count as the goal.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Annotating every obvious local while leaving public inputs and return values unclear.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that a typed boundary gives the checker information that can flow into the implementation and its callers.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Prioritize function parameters, return values, class fields, and shared module variables.
Annotate empty collections when their future element type is not inferable.
Let the checker infer obvious locals such as `count = 0`.
Use an annotation when it documents a wider interface than the current value suggests.
More annotations are not automatically better; useful contracts are the goal.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Type annotations are most valuable where one part of a program hands data to another part. Public functions, service methods, class fields, configuration objects, and library APIs all benefit because both callers and implementations can be checked against the same contract.

I also annotate values that begin without enough information for inference. For example, `names: list[str] = []` tells the checker what may be appended even though the empty list itself has no element from which to infer `str`.

I do not repeat types that are already obvious. In `attempts = 0`, a checker can infer `int`; writing the annotation again usually adds noise unless the variable deliberately needs a broader type such as `int | None`.

An explicit annotation can document an interface that is wider than one implementation value. A parameter typed as `Sequence[str]` can accept a list or tuple even if every current caller happens to pass a list.

The boundary is that hints only improve safety when the project actually runs a checker, and they cannot prove business rules such as a positive price or a valid email address. Those still need validation and tests.

sections.title: Think in information boundaries
sections.content:
A checker builds knowledge from declarations and inference. An annotated function gives it facts about values entering the body and about the value that must leave. Those facts then help it inspect every expression and every checked caller. One useful boundary annotation can therefore protect more code than several annotations on temporary variables.

Inference works best when the value is immediate and precise. A literal, constructor call, or well-typed function result often supplies all the information needed. It becomes weak around empty containers, `None`, changing branches, external data, and deliberately broad interfaces. That is where a written annotation resolves ambiguity.

Runtime data is a separate concern. JSON, environment variables, database rows, and HTTP payloads can violate a hint because they enter from outside the static program. Parse and validate those values at the boundary, then pass a well-typed model further into the application.

sections.title: Annotate the contract, infer the obvious
sections.content:
| Code location | Better default | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Public parameter or return | Annotate | Defines the interface for both sides |
| Empty collection | Annotate | No element exists to infer from |
| Simple local literal | Infer | The assigned value already gives a precise type |
| Data from JSON or a request | Validate, then annotate/model | External values are not made safe by a hint |
| Deliberately broad variable | Annotate | The initial value may be narrower than the real contract |

sections.title: Use annotations where inference runs out
sections.content:
```python
from collections.abc import Sequence

def normalized_names(names: Sequence[str]) -> list[str]:
    result: list[str] = []  # the empty list needs an element type
    for name in names:
        cleaned = name.strip()  # `cleaned` is inferred as str
        if cleaned:
            result.append(cleaned)
    return result

print(normalized_names((" Ada ", "", "Lin")))
```

The signature documents a flexible boundary, the empty output gets an explicit element type, and the obvious loop local is left to inference.

questions.question: Do Python type annotations reject values of the wrong type at runtime?
questions.title: Type Hints Are Not Runtime Enforcement
questions.direct_answer: No. Standard Python does not reject a function argument or assignment merely because it disagrees with an annotation. A static checker can report the mismatch before execution, while runtime enforcement requires explicit validation or a library that performs it.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you separate static type checking from runtime validation.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Trusting an annotation at an API boundary and using unvalidated input as if Python had checked it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name all three layers: annotations describe a contract, a checker analyses code, and validation protects runtime boundaries.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Annotations alone do not block wrong argument or assignment types.
A static checker reports mismatches without running the program.
Python still raises normal runtime errors when an invalid operation is eventually attempted.
External data needs parsing and validation even when the destination is annotated.
Frameworks may enforce hints, but that enforcement belongs to the framework.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Python type annotations do not enforce a function contract by themselves. The interpreter normally stores the hints, accepts the objects passed by the caller, and executes the function using those objects' real runtime types.

A static checker is what catches the disagreement early. For example, mypy can report a call to `double("4")` when `double` expects an `int`, even though ordinary Python will still make the call if that code is run.

The program may appear to work or may fail later. Multiplying a string by two is legal, so a bad call can even return `"44"`; another operation might raise `TypeError`. This is why a hint is not a security or data-validation boundary.

Values from requests, JSON, databases, or user input must be parsed and checked at runtime. A framework may inspect annotations and perform that work, but it is extra behaviour supplied by the framework.

I use annotations plus a checker for developer feedback, tests for behaviour, and runtime validation for untrusted data. Each layer solves a different problem.

sections.title: Static promise versus runtime evidence
sections.content:
A static checker reasons about source code and declared types. It can follow known calls, assignments, branches, and return statements, but it does not inspect the actual request that will arrive tomorrow. Runtime validation examines a real value at the moment it crosses a boundary.

This separation is intentional: Python remains dynamically typed, and annotations can also be consumed by documentation tools, serializers, dependency-injection systems, and other libraries. The interpreter cannot assume that every annotation should act as a mandatory validator.

Even `typing.cast()` does not validate or convert a value. It returns the same object and asks the checker to trust the programmer's claim. Use `isinstance`, parsing logic, a schema/model library, or a domain constructor when runtime proof is required.

sections.title: Three different safety layers
sections.content:
| Layer | When it works | What it catches | What it cannot guarantee |
|---|---|---|---|
| Type annotation | In source code | Describes the intended contract | Nothing is rejected by itself |
| Static checker | Before execution | Inconsistent checked code paths | Unknown future input and unchecked code |
| Runtime validation | During execution | Actual invalid external values | Every later business behaviour |

sections.title: See the wrong type pass the call boundary
sections.content:
```python
def double(value: int) -> int:
    return value * 2

print(double(4))
print(double("4"))  # runs and prints 44; a checker flags this call

def parse_count(raw: object) -> int:
    if not isinstance(raw, int):
        raise TypeError("count must be an int")
    return raw

print(parse_count(4))
```

The annotation helps static analysis; the explicit `isinstance` branch is the runtime check.

followup_questions: What is the difference between mypy and runtime validation?
Does `typing.cast()` check or convert a value?
Why can a wrong typed call sometimes appear to work?
